title: Does design matter? Jason Cohen on WP Engine's redesign, ITWatchDogs and deciding where design fits your strategy
summary: Jason Cohen shows that a full WP Engine redesign didn't move bounce rate, time-on-site or conversion. Smart Bear and ITWatchDogs grew fast with ugly sites, while Hipmunk won on design alone. His conclusion is to decide whether design is core to your identity and act consistently. If it isn't, nail something else harder.

principles.text: A full redesign can delight customers and staff yet leave bounce rate, time-on-site and conversion unchanged. Measure before assuming design drives growth.
principles.quote: Hmm. Looks like the data are objectively saying "design doesn't matter."

principles.text: Subjective signals count even when metrics don't move: embarrassed staff, customers who wince referring you, and a bigger customer judging you mature.
principles.quote: But as much as I respect Lean Startup theory, objective measurements aren't the only things that matter.

principles.text: Ugly sites can still grow fast. Smart Bear doubled revenue and profit yearly for five years, and ITWatchDogs grew every month to a successful exit.
principles.quote: This doesn't prove design *doesn't* matter, but it does suggest design may not be the deciding factor.

principles.text: When design is your core strategy, how you win and acquire customers, it can be the most important thing. Hipmunk's only edge was a quantum leap in design.
principles.quote: When design is fundamental to the strategy--how you _win_, how you acquire and retain customers, garner attention and referrals, and be distinguished in the market--then design can be the most important thing.

principles.text: Message and brand fit can beat polish. ITWatchDogs' messy site matched its low-cost, relatable culture and customers' cluttered offices, and the message was clear.
principles.quote: The site might have *looked bad*, but our message couldn't have been clearer.

principles.text: Decide whether design is core to your startup's identity, then act consistently. If it's not, nail your real strengths harder, since design-led rivals will mask their weak spots.
principles.quote: if design is not important to you, you'd better decide what *is* important and **nail those things all the harder**
